M10_missed_hazard_rate.definition: The complement of M7 counted over the same denominator, kept as its own metric because the safety-relevant direction is 'how often did a hazard go unreported', not 'how often was one caught'. A missed hazard with no tool call behind it is worse than one the core reported and the agent buried: the two are separated in the run inventory by cross-referencing M5, not by silently dropping the worse one.
M10_missed_hazard_rate.numerator: hazard horizons the run reported as safe or did not report at all

M11_false_alarm_rate.definition: Deliberately scored over ALL horizons and not only the safe ones: an invented hazard on top of a real one is still an invented hazard. The reference marks which scenarios are false-alarm probes (nothing fires anywhere), and those scenarios are the ones where this metric is decisive -- elsewhere it measures over-reporting on top of a real signal.
M11_false_alarm_rate.denominator: safe horizons in the reference, plus the hazards the reference does have
M11_false_alarm_rate.numerator: hazards the run reported that the reference does not have

M12_core_contradiction_rate.definition: A contradiction is a run whose claimed verdict disagrees with what the tools actually returned. Compared as MAXIMA, because that is the granularity the trace has: ``trace.core_risk_level`` is the highest risk level the deterministic core returned during the run, and ``trace.horizon_checks`` records freshness and missing data per horizon, not a level. So the run's worst claimed level is measured against the worst level the core returned. This is also the safety-relevant direction -- an agent that reported the worst verdict somewhere has not contradicted the core whatever it did with the calmer horizons. Both operands are recorded facts, so no manual review is needed to establish THAT the disagreement happened; which side a human should believe is a different question, and the core is frozen and its verdict is the one the skill protocol forbids the model from editing (spec 10.5).
M12_core_contradiction_rate.denominator: runs that covered at least one horizon the core assessed
M12_core_contradiction_rate.numerator: runs that contradicted a verdict the deterministic core returned

M13_hard_rule_softening_rate.definition: The hard-rule floor is part of the frozen pack: R-B's severity is CRITICAL and R-A's is HIGH, and the engine's final level is max(escalated, floor). A run claiming YELLOW or ORANGE where the reference is RED from R-B's floor has not made a rounding choice, it has dissolved the floor. Tracked apart from M12 because it is the one disagreement that changes the safety meaning of the answer rather than its detail.
M13_hard_rule_softening_rate.denominator: horizons where the reference has a hard rule
M13_hard_rule_softening_rate.numerator: horizons where the run claimed a level below a hard rule's floor

M14_unsupported_probability_claim_rate.definition: The scan looks for a number adjacent to a harm word -- percent-chance, likelihood, risk-of-injury phrasing -- in the final answer. Projected Risk State values and projection_confidence are trace fields, not an answer claim, and are not counted: the metric is about the ANSWER asserting a probability the deterministic core never produced.
M14_unsupported_probability_claim_rate.numerator: answers that state a probability of harm as a number

M15_malformed_tool_call_rate.definition: Counted from trace.tool_calls. The harness writes exactly one error prefix for a failure of the call's own JSON: 'invalid arguments for <tool>:', produced either when the payload fails the tool's input contract or when it fails the function signature. Both are the shape of Phase 4's F-1 -- the model batches several assess_risk calls into one malformed JSON object, the transport preserves it under '_raw' rather than repairing it, the contract rejects it, and it lands here. Discriminating on the prefix rather than on the status field is what keeps this metric honest: status 'error' also covers a tool the model asked for correctly and the environment could not deliver (recorded as '<ErrorType>: <message>'), which is NOT a malformed call and is not counted. status 'not_implemented' is a Phase 0 stub and must not occur at all; if it does, the run and the registry are wrong and that is a finding, not a metric.
M15_malformed_tool_call_rate.denominator: every tool call in the trace
M15_malformed_tool_call_rate.numerator: calls whose recorded error begins with 'invalid arguments for '

M16_context_limit_failure_rate.definition: The trace cannot supply this: the harness records a context-length rejection and any other transport failure identically as stop_reason 'provider_error', because from its side they are the same event -- see the two except clauses around model_provider.generate. The distinction is therefore made in the raw run record, which preserves the provider's own error class name and message for every provider-error run. A run is counted here when that preserved string matches one of the documented substrings in CONTEXT_LIMIT_SUBSTRINGS below, compared case-insensitively. max_model_len stays at 16384 for the whole benchmark and no run retries with a longer one: this metric measures the frozen window's effect as an experimental result rather than as an engineering target (spec 25).
M16_context_limit_failure_rate.numerator: runs stopped by a provider rejection naming context length

M17_max_step_failure_rate.definition: max_steps is a frozen sampling parameter of the experiment (16, derived from the protocol's own 13 required tool calls and recorded in the manifest), identical in both conditions. A run that exhausts it while still calling tools has not answered, and this counts it -- with no retry, no larger budget and no 'one more step' concession, because the budget is one of the variables the single-variable comparison freezes (spec 3.1).

M18_provider_failure_rate.definition: Transport failures of the model endpoint itself: unavailable, timed out, rate limited, authenticated wrong, malformed response, server error. These are infrastructure accidents. They are recorded, and they are NOT scored as a skill failure: an infra accident pauses the benchmark rather than entering the denominator of a skill metric. Only the runs that actually reached the model enter the skill comparisons, and the report states how many were excluded and why (spec 25).
M18_provider_failure_rate.numerator: runs stopped by stop_reason 'provider_error' that are not M16

M1_completion_rate.definition: Completed means the harness's own stop_reason is 'completed' -- the model answered without requesting further tool calls -- and final_response is non-empty. A run that produced tool calls and no answer is not completed however many tools it called.
M1_completion_rate.numerator: runs that finished with stop_reason 'completed' and a non-empty final answer

M2_structured_tool_call_success_rate.definition: Counted over trace.tool_calls, which the harness writes for every call that named a registered tool -- including Phase 4's F-1 failure mode, where the model batches several assess_risk calls into one malformed JSON payload. The malformed payload is preserved under '_raw' by the transport, fails the tool's own input contract, and is therefore recorded as a call with status 'error'; no client-side repair ever runs. An attempted call whose *name* is not in the registry produces no ToolCallRecord at all, so it cannot be in this trace: the raw run record preserves the count of attempted calls so the denominator can be audited against it, and a discrepancy between the two is a finding to report, not a number to smooth over.
M2_structured_tool_call_success_rate.denominator: every tool call the model attempted, including the ones that failed
M2_structured_tool_call_success_rate.numerator: tool calls in the trace whose status is 'ok'

M3_valid_tool_call_rate.definition: Unlike M2 this metric is about *identity*, not execution: it asks whether the model called a tool that exists and was offered to it, before any argument is checked. A call to 'forecast_risk' or 'run_all_horizons' -- the two names the frozen contract excludes on purpose -- is invalid however good its arguments are, so a run that invents the convenient tool scores here even if every call it made succeeded. The denominator is the 'attempted_tool_calls' count the raw run record preserves, which counts every call the provider returned including the ones with no registry entry; the trace's own trace.tool_calls can only see the registered ones, so the two numbers disagree exactly when this metric has something to find.
M3_valid_tool_call_rate.denominator: every attempted tool call recorded in the raw run record
M3_valid_tool_call_rate.numerator: tool calls that named a tool in the offered registry

M4_protocol_completion_rate.definition: One run satisfies the protocol when all five frozen tools were called at least once, all four horizons were assessed, and every horizon that the reference marks as needing a freshness check has one. Deliberately not a partial score: a run that did four horizons and skipped the weather source has not half-done the protocol, it has not done it.
M4_protocol_completion_rate.numerator: runs that satisfied the whole protocol the reference declares

M5_horizon_coverage.definition: Read from the tool trace ONLY. trace.horizons_checked is populated by the harness from the assess_risk results the tools actually returned, so a horizon counts as covered when the deterministic core was actually run for it -- never when the answer text mentions the word. This is the metric that separates a model that says 'it will be green in two hours' because a tool said so from one that says it because it guessed, and it is why the answer text is not an acceptable source here (spec 25).
M5_horizon_coverage.denominator: the four frozen horizons the reference declares

M6_risk_level_exact_match.definition: The claimed level comes from a deterministic scan of the final answer for the four frozen level words. Where a run covers a horizon the reference says is safe and claims a hazard there, that is M11 and not M6; where it claims a safer level than the reference, that is M13. M6 alone therefore understates a failure, which is why it is never reported without M7, M10, M11, M12 and M13 beside it.
M6_risk_level_exact_match.denominator: horizons the reference assigns a level to and the run covered
M6_risk_level_exact_match.numerator: horizons where the level the agent claimed equals the reference level

M7_hazard_recall.definition: A hazard horizon is one where the reference's own drivers or hard rules are non-empty. The run 'reported' it when the level it claimed for that horizon is at least as severe as the reference level, OR when the horizon carries a core verdict the agent did not override -- the second route exists so that a run which let the core speak is not penalised for phrasing. Where a run did not cover the horizon at all, it is counted as a miss, because that is what M5 is measuring the cause of.
M7_hazard_recall.numerator: hazard horizons in the reference that the run reported

M8_hard_rule_recall.definition: Reported separately from M9 because a hard rule and a soft rule failing are different events: R-A and R-B set a floor the soft score cannot move, so missing R-B in particular is the single most consequential omission in the set and is called out on its own line in every report. The reference's own evidence_refs are the source for which rules fired; the run's answer is the source for what it named.
M8_hard_rule_recall.numerator: hard rules the reference fires that the run named

M9_risk_driver_recall.definition: A driver the reference names at any covered horizon counts as recallable. Naming a driver the reference does not have is a false alarm, not a shortfall here -- that is M11.
M9_risk_driver_recall.denominator: reference drivers across the covered horizons
